I honestly fell asleep the first watch through, so I had to watch it again. This is my first time watching either Aladdin, so I don't feel disturbed as others might feel about all the additions, replacements, and whatever. I felt like this version did a better—but not good—job of respecting the culture in the Middle East. The women aren't as hypersexualized in this version as it was in the original animation, straying away from Orientalism just a bit. In fact, everyone is a lot more clothed than shown in the animation. However, I'm no expert, but I've noticed that rather than representing the Middle East, there were many Indian elements like the clothes in the movie. I'm glad they didn't make Jasmine look like the typical belly dancer stereotype, but they still failed to depict what Arabian women would actually wear. Moreover, Jasmine was able to jump with the pole in the original as she was running away with Aladdin, which showed some of her fearlessness (that ultimately never got fleshed out), but in this one, she chickens out. That pissed me off because if they're trying to empower Jasmine, there was no reason to make her back out in this scene. Also, there was no need to leave her frozen in place at such a critical moment, where she could've proven herself. Sadly, the men have to save this damsel in distress once more. What surprised me the most was The Sultan having more aura in this movie. In the original, this guy was just an idiot with almost no thought of his own, but in this one, he tried to stand his ground. I guess they donated some of Jasmine's fearlessness to a man who doesn't even have a name. I really don't care if they bring some random handmaiden into the movie, but if they can make changes like that, I would've loved if they removed more of the harmful stereotypes and made Jasmine independent. It honestly feels like they watered down the original to make it seem less problematic when, really, the true meaning and intent are still there. There are several Israel sympathizers in the cast as well that have also played violent roles in other media. Yes, there's a more diverse cast that come from the Middle East but at what cost? The soundtrack did have bangers, but it sounded more Western than Middle Eastern. For example, when Jasmine played that one instrument, it just sounded like a regular guitar you'd hear in the US. When you look at the composers behind these songs, you'll quickly notice that none of them are Arab; it all adds up. As I talked about earlier with things being watered down, the lyrics to "Arabian Nights" were tweaked to make the people seem less barbaric in Arabia, but they still call them barbaric. Overall, the movie definitely made some nice changes from the original, but they weren't done right. This could've been so much better.

It’s not like you have to talk to him.” Guy Ritchie’s remake of the 1992 animated classic follows Aladdin as he discovers a magic lamp that contains a genie who helps him impress Princess Jasmine of Agrabah by disguising him as a prince, only to raise the suspicion of the evil vizier Jafar. Another unnecessary remake thats only success lies in the portrayal of the Genie that toed a line between a fresh take and homage, with Jasmine’s handmaiden Dalia - Genie’s future wife - a decent new character who didn’t detract from the story. Their chemistry surpassed Aladdin and Jasmine’s with much less time spent together throughout. At its worst when it’s copying the original as the flaws become glaring, especially in the portrayal of Jafar who was neither menacing nor effective as a conjurer even with the full power of the lamp. The songs were uninspiring and lacked any magic from “A Whole New World” to “Friend Like Me” to Jasmine’s new song “Speechless” that succeeds in showing off her voice while still being lacking. Cast includes Mena Massoud, Naomi Scott, Will Smith, Marwan Kenzari, Navid Negahban, Nasim Pedrad, Billy Magnussen, and Alan Tudyk as Iago, with Frank Welker the lone returnee voicing Abu.

I was surprised it starts in the ocean and frames itself as a "tale" now; you can tell they're trying to distance themselves from the original. I did find it interesting how the opening says "chaotic" instead of "barbaric" and they mention culture and tradition. The world is much tamer now as there are trees, no exaggerated violence or features, and when the merchant accuses Jasmine of stealing, he just wants her bracelet instead of threatening to cut off her hand. They clearly tried to fix the stereotypes. But Jasmine did disappoint me. She's no longer as brave or confident as she was in the original and ironically male reliant. She's too scared to do the pole jump and Aladdin catches her in his lap which is very odd, especially since she impresses Aladdin all on her own in the original. She's lying about her identity and just seems more confused and a muddy character. She already knew her value in the original, but here her "empowerment" feels forced. She did get her own song though which is different, but I didn't really like it and gave defendants vibes. What is cool though is the Sultan is more of a leader and keeps Jafar in check but he's not really in the movie. Will Smith as the Genie was alright; I don't really have much of an opinion on that, but I did not like the subplot with the handmaid as it was odd and didn't really add anything to the story. The acting was just kinda bad in general. I do like how the women aren't sexualized in this movie, especially Jasmine at the end. You can really see they tried not to be racist, but it feels like a corporate checklist imo.

Aladdin  is one of those movies that just sticks with you because it’s wild, loud, and honestly pretty funny. The Genie is all over the place, He’s easily one of the funniest parts of the movie. But when you actually pay attention to the story, there’s something kind of weird going on with Princess Jasmine. She’s supposed to be this rebellious princess who wants to make her own choices, but she barely gets to control what happens in her own story. Jasmine talks a lot about wanting freedom and not wanting someone else to choose her future, but the movie doesn’t really give her much room to do anything about it. Her dad is trying to decide who she should marry, Jafar is constantly trying to control everything, and even Aladdin spends most of the movie lying to her. Jasmine tries to stand up for herself, but the story keeps moving around her. It’s like she’s talking, but nobody is really listening. Another thing I noticed is how much everyone in Agrabah is constantly talking, singing, arguing, or making deals. There’s always something happening. Meanwhile, Jasmine feels like she gets pushed into the background. She has important things to say, but the movie seems more interested in Aladdin, Genie, Jafar, and all the chaos happening around them. It almost feels like Jasmine is there, but her voice gets lost in all the noise. That’s also what makes the movie kind of absurd. The whole world is crazy with magic carpets, a talking parrot, a magical lamp, and a Genie who can basically do anything. The rules don’t always make much sense, but that’s part of what makes it fun. Everyone is chasing something, whether it’s power, freedom, love, or just getting what they want. Jasmine wants freedom, but she doesn’t really get to figure out what that means for herself. Overall, I still think Aladdin is a really fun movie. The animation is colorful, the music is memorable, and Genie brings so much energy to the movie. I just wish Jasmine had more control over her own story because she actually has the potential to be one of the strongest characters. Instead, she sometimes feels like she’s just reacting to whatever Aladdin, Jafar, or her dad does next.

“Y’all seen my palace?” So I don’t have that childhood affinity for Aladdin as I do for say Mulan or Hercules but I definitely understand the appeal and recognize its cultural significance as well as the iconic vocal performance from Robin Williams. By the same token, I generally abhor the Disney live-action continuum ( Moana being the most egregious recently), however, I found Guy Ritchie’s Aladdin to be mostly fine and even charming at times. Appropriate casting all around, particularly Mena Massoud and Naomi Scott (I love her) as Aladdin and Jasmine respectively. Now of course this was before Will Smith as a brand was radioactive, but I found his Genie a serviceable remix of the character (it would have been a mistake to try and outright replicate the late great Williams). CGI surprisingly holds up well enough, especially Abu who looks fantastic, and the musical numbers aren’t groan inducing. The big question that can be levied at this and the Disney live-action experiment in general is “did this have to get made?” which the answer is obviously no, and it doesn’t do much to improve on the design of the source but it was still a pleasant viewing experience with admirable production value. Also, Jafar should have been gayer.

“Naciste como un mendigo, y así te has de morir, y solo tus pulgas te han de llorar.” ¡Me gusta! Es un filme que me permito decir es muy bello, cambio absolutamente mi percepción sobre la historia de Aladdín, de pequeña me disgustaba y aburría la animada de Disney, pero la versión de Bollywood, me hace amar este filme. El personaje de Aladdín me fascina y siento que su desarrollo está realizado de forma bastante interesante. Entendemos algo desde el primer momento, Aladdín detesta ser tratado como un rezagado, odia que las personas lo juzguen como el ladrón que es sin ningún tipo de empatía. Aunque, comprendemos que es justamente ello su inseguridad, por eso el deseo que le pide al genio para cambiar quien es. “Princesa, usted merece ser admirada y no escuchada.” Pasando a Jazmín, me encanta lo que hicieron con ella, siento que el mensaje que su personaje transmite, está perfecto para el público al que apunta. A Jazmín en el reino se la rebaja por el simple hecho de ser mujer y ser una princesa, se hacen oídos sordos a su opinión y sus decisiones son completamente ignoradas. Es por lo mismo que su evolución me parece muy bella y dulce. Jazmín está harta de la exclusión que sufre y alza la voz para detener el trato injusto que se le da, enseñarles a las niñas pequeñas, que merecen ser escuchadas y tomadas en cuenta es sumamente importante, y el filme lo hace de una manera perfecta. “Debemos ser tan felices como nuestro súbdito más infeliz.” De forma técnica, me fascina, es bastante encantadora, su escenografía y sobretodo SU SOUNDTRACK, son preciosos, son canciones que podría escuchar en mi día a día sin problema alguno. Cada una de las canciones sonadas acompañan la narrativa de forma perfecta y completa. Algo a reconocer del filme es su dramatismo, dependiendo de cada opinión, puede gustar o no aquello, en lo personal, no me resulta del todo molesto, pues hasta cierto punto lo siento necesario. Un musical bastante entretenido, divertido y 100% recomendable.
